known_pitfalls.claim: Magnification and resolution mean the same thing.
known_pitfalls.correction: Magnification tells how many times larger the image appears; resolution tells the smallest separation at which two points can still be distinguished. A larger blurred image does not contain more resolved detail.

known_pitfalls.claim: Adding stronger lenses to a school microscope will allow it to reveal arbitrarily small objects.
known_pitfalls.correction: A light microscope is limited to about 0.2 µm resolution by diffraction, so additional magnification beyond useful resolution produces empty magnification.

known_pitfalls.claim: The objective and eyepiece magnifications should be added.
known_pitfalls.correction: Total magnification is their product: M = m_o × m_e.

known_pitfalls.claim: The final image in a compound microscope is upright relative to the original specimen.
known_pitfalls.correction: The objective forms a real inverted intermediate image, and the eyepiece magnifies it into a virtual image that remains inverted relative to the original specimen.

known_pitfalls.claim: A coarse adjustment knob should be used for focusing under high power.
known_pitfalls.correction: Coarse adjustment is for rough focusing at low power; fine adjustment is used for sharp focus at high power to reduce the risk of the objective striking the slide.

known_pitfalls.claim: A temporary mount can be preserved for years if it is covered carefully.
known_pitfalls.correction: Water dries, cells shrink, and stain may crystallise; long-term storage requires fixation, staining, dehydration, and sealing in a mounting medium such as Canada balsam or DPX.

known_pitfalls.claim: TEM is best for 3D-like surface views and SEM is best for internal ultrastructure.
known_pitfalls.correction: TEM transmits electrons through ultrathin sections to show internal details in 2D; SEM scans the surface to produce 3D-like surface images.

known_pitfalls.claim: Electron microscopes can routinely observe living cells.
known_pitfalls.correction: TEM and SEM require vacuum and extensive preparation; these conditions kill cells, so living specimens are observed with suitable light microscopes.

recommended_example_progression: Use the two-dot observation in Section 9.1 to explain the human-eye resolution limit of about 0.1 mm at 25 cm.
Use Activity 9.2 to build a timeline including Janssen, Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Abbe, Ruska, and Zernike.
Use Activity 9.3 and Fig. 9.4 to identify the parts of a compound microscope and connect each part with its role.
Use Activities 9.4 and 9.5 to compare temporary and permanent mounts without inventing observations not recorded by the student.
Use Section 9.4.3 examples to calculate 400X total magnification, 0.05 mm actual cell size, 150X magnification, and 0.2 mm cell size from field of view.
Use Check Your Understanding Q1 and Q6 for total magnification, cell-size estimation, and inverse field-of-view calculation.
Use Check Your Understanding Q2, Q8, and Q10 to select phase-contrast, TEM, or SEM according to whether the specimen is living, internal, or a surface.
Use Check Your Understanding Q3 and Q13 to distinguish magnification from resolution and explain empty magnification.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter ends with 'Check Your Understanding', questions 1-15, covering calculations, instrument selection, slide preparation, resolution, applications, and microscopy care.

beyond_the_textbook: Confocal microscopy uses focused illumination and optical sectioning to build clearer images from different depths in a fluorescent specimen.
Super-resolution light microscopy uses specialised methods to localise fluorescent signals more precisely than an ordinary light microscope can resolve.

Cryo-electron microscopy rapidly freezes specimens so biological structures can be studied in a near-native state without the usual heavy staining, although the specimens are not alive during imaging.
Digital image analysis can measure cell size, count objects, and compare brightness, but accurate conclusions still depend on calibration and good specimen preparation.
Microscope images may contain artefacts caused by preparation, staining, focus, or detector processing, so scientists compare controls and repeat observations.
